lead: This unit shows what a cloud service stands on: networks, data centres, web protocols, service contracts, elastic capacity, replication and written promises. After it you can trace one request from a phone to a data centre, size an auto-scaling rule, compute service availability, and read an SLA without confusion.
about: Unit 2 follows the request from the wire to the bill. Chapter 2.1 starts with networks, ISPs and data centres: the physical path and the power that make a cloud region. Chapter 2.2 adds web protocols and multitenancy, so one running service can serve many customers safely. Chapter 2.3 turns those services into contracts with SOA and REST. Chapter 2.4 makes capacity follow demand through automated scaling. Chapter 2.5 spreads traffic and keeps replicas, so failures do not stop service. Chapter 2.6 writes the promises down as SLAs and SLOs. Chapter 2.7, taught in only a few universities, closes with virtual servers, storage devices and usage monitors that feed the invoice.

chapters.idea: A cloud region is a building full of racks, switches and power, reached through a chain of ISPs, and that physical path sets latency and availability.
chapters.depth: Access network, ISP hierarchy (tier 1, tier 2, tier 3), transit and peering, internet exchange points, last mile, latency versus bandwidth. Data centre: racks, top-of-rack switch, aggregation and core switches, servers, power distribution, cooling, PUE, redundancy N+1 and 2N, regions and availability zones. Some syllabi call this public cloud infrastructure. Keep protocol details at the level of names and roles.

figure.title: One request path into a cloud region
figure.aria: A phone reaches its local ISP, then transit and an internet exchange, then the cloud region, the top-of-rack switch and a server rack.

chapters.example: A Chennai user talks to a Mumbai region 1,200 km away over fibre at 2×10⁸ m/s. The access network adds 5 ms, ISP hops add 2 ms, and data centre switching adds 0.5 ms. Find the one-way delay and the round-trip time. The data centre draws 1.5 MW for IT equipment at PUE 1.4 and pays ₹8 per kWh. Find its monthly energy cost for 730 hours. Answer: fibre time = 1,200,000 m ÷ 2×10⁸ m/s = 6 ms; one way = 6 + 5 + 2 + 0.5 = 13.5 ms; RTT = 27 ms. Total power = 1.5 MW × 1.4 = 2.1 MW; energy = 2.1 MW × 730 h = 1,533 MWh = 1,533,000 kWh; cost = 1,533,000 × ₹8 = ₹1,22,64,000, about ₹1.23 crore.
chapters.trap: Bandwidth is not latency: a fat link can still be far away. PUE is total facility power divided by IT power, not the other way round.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for cloud regions, deployment models and the NIST view.
chapters.leave: Hypervisor and VM internals to Unit 3; storage organisation to Unit 4; packet-level protocol details to a networking course.

chapters.idea: Users reach cloud software through HTTP and DNS, and multitenancy lets one running stack serve many customers with logical separation.
chapters.depth: DNS lookup, HTTP request and response, stateless HTTP, cookies and sessions, TLS handshake outline, web servers and application servers, JSON and HTML. Multitenancy models: shared database with tenant_id, separate schemas, separate databases; tenant-aware caching; noisy-neighbour effects; logical network perimeter as a per-tenant boundary. Examples: CRM, social feeds, media streaming, online gaming. Some syllabi call the isolation boundary a logical network perimeter.

figure.aria: A browser looks up the site in DNS, sends an HTTP request with a session cookie, the app finds tenant 42 and queries only that tenant's rows.

chapters.example: A SaaS order table has 1,000,000 rows shared by 500 tenants. (a) How many rows does a query scan with no tenant filter? (b) With an index on (tenant_id, id), roughly how many rows does one tenant query scan? (c) What is the reduction factor? Answer: (a) 1,000,000 rows. (b) 1,000,000 ÷ 500 = 2,000 rows on average. (c) 1,000,000 ÷ 2,000 = 500 times fewer rows.
chapters.trap: Multitenancy does not mean one machine per customer. The common failure is a query or cache key that forgets tenant_id and leaks another tenant's data.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for the network path; Unit 1 for SaaS and the cloud reference model.
chapters.leave: REST constraints and idempotency to chapter 2.3; TLS encryption and identity to Unit 6; container isolation to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: SOA packages function as loosely coupled services with standard contracts, and REST is the lightweight HTTP style most cloud APIs use.
chapters.depth: SOA principles: loose coupling, abstraction, reuse, autonomy, statelessness, discoverability. Service registry, orchestration versus choreography, enterprise service bus, SOAP, WSDL, UDDI, XML. REST constraints: client-server, stateless, cacheable, uniform interface, layered system, code on demand. Resources, URIs, HTTP verbs, status codes, idempotency, JSON. REST versus SOAP. Microservices as a descendant of SOA.

figure.aria: A five-layer service stack: presentation, process, services, messaging and data, with the service layer picked out.

chapters.example: A client sends POST /payments for ₹500. The response is lost, so the client retries twice, three attempts in total, with the same Idempotency-Key. Without the key the customer is debited 3 × ₹500 = ₹1,500. With the key the server stores the first result and returns it again: one debit of ₹500 and two replays of the stored response. If the server keeps keys for 24 hours and a retry arrives after 25 hours, it is treated as a new request and can debit again.
chapters.trap: REST is an architectural style, not a protocol, and it does not require XML. PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, so retries need an idempotency key.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.2 for HTTP verbs, status codes and statelessness.
chapters.leave: SOAP security and WS-Security to Unit 6; microservice deployment and containers to Unit 3 and Unit 5; API gateway products to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Elasticity adds or removes capacity automatically from measured demand, inside minimum and maximum limits.
chapters.depth: Elasticity versus scalability; vertical scaling up and down; horizontal scaling out and in; on-demand versus reserved capacity. Auto-scaling parts: metric collection, rule or target, minimum, maximum, cooldown, warm pool, health check. Policies: target tracking, step scaling, scheduled and predictive scaling. Metrics: CPU, queue length, requests per second. Thrashing and flapping. Some syllabi call the rule engine an automated scaling listener.

figure.title: Auto-scaling control loop
figure.aria: A loop from metrics to a rule check, scaling out, a cooldown, steady state, and back to metrics.

chapters.example: A web app peaks at 600 requests per second. Each server handles 100 requests per second at full load, and the target is 60% utilisation, so each server is kept at 60 requests per second. Required servers = 600 ÷ 60 = 10. The base is 2 servers. At ₹9 per server-hour: base 2 servers for 24 h cost 2 × 24 × ₹9 = ₹432; the 8 extra servers run for 4 peak hours and cost 8 × 4 × ₹9 = ₹288; total ₹720. Running 10 servers for 24 h costs 10 × 24 × ₹9 = ₹2,160, so the saving is ₹1,440.
chapters.trap: Without a cooldown the group flaps, adding and removing servers every minute. Average CPU can also hide one hot instance that needs scaling.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.1 for data centre capacity; Unit 4 for provisioning and scheduling policies.
chapters.leave: Placement and scheduling algorithms to Unit 4; traffic distribution to chapter 2.5; cost models and billing to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A load balancer spreads requests over healthy replicas, and replication plus failover keeps service alive when a copy fails.
chapters.depth: Algorithms: round robin, weighted round robin, least connections, least response time, IP hash. Layer 4 versus layer 7 balancing, health checks, sticky sessions, session stores. Replication: synchronous and asynchronous, primary-replica, read replicas, quorum, replication lag. High availability: active-passive and active-active, failover system, redundancy, availability arithmetic. Keep RTO and RPO definitions short; metrics go deeper in chapter 2.6.

figure.title: Balanced web tier with a replicated database
figure.aria: A client reaches a load balancer that sends traffic to two healthy servers and skips a failed third; the healthy servers write to a primary database that copies asynchronously to a replica.

chapters.example: Three web servers each have availability 0.99 and sit behind one load balancer with availability 0.999. The servers fail independently, and the service works if the load balancer works and at least one server works. Find service availability and yearly downtime in 8,760 hours. Answer: server group = 1 − (1 − 0.99)³ = 1 − 0.01³ = 0.999999. Service = 0.999 × 0.999999 = 0.998999001, about 99.90%. Downtime = (1 − 0.998999001) × 8,760 = 8.77 hours per year. The load balancer is now the bottleneck.
chapters.trap: Available components in series multiply, so a 99.9% load balancer can cap the whole service. A parallel group is 1 minus the product of its failure probabilities, not the sum of availabilities.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.4 for adding instances; chapter 2.1 for regions and zones.
chapters.leave: GFS and HDFS replica placement to Unit 4; fault-tolerance theory and business continuity to Unit 4; SLA credits to chapter 2.6.

chapters.idea: An SLA is the contract customers can claim against, and an SLO is the stricter internal target that leaves room before the contract breaks.
chapters.depth: Definitions: SLI is the measured number, SLO is the target, SLA is the agreement with consequences. SLA parts: parties, service description, metrics, measurement window, exclusions, support, credits or penalties. Availability in nines and allowed downtime. Error budget. Composite SLA for services in series. RTO and RPO as recovery promises. Monitoring and reporting. Do not quote provider-specific percentages as universal facts.

figure.title: From measurement to promise
figure.aria: A service is measured as an SLI, checked against an SLO, converted into an error budget, and compared with the SLA; a monitor feeds the SLI.

chapters.example: A 30-day month has 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes. An SLA of 99.9% allows 43,200 × 0.001 = 43.2 minutes of downtime. An SLO of 99.95% allows 43,200 × 0.0005 = 21.6 minutes. Actual downtime is 30 minutes: the SLO is breached but the SLA is met, so releases are frozen but no credit is due. Two services in series with 99.9% and 99.95% give 0.999 × 0.9995 = 0.9985005, about 99.85%, which allows 43,200 × 0.0014995 = 64.8 minutes.
chapters.trap: An SLO must be stricter than the SLA, otherwise there is no warning before credits are due. Composite availability is the product of the parts, not the minimum.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2.5 for availability and replication; Unit 1 for service models.
chapters.leave: Contract law and credit calculation to Unit 4 billing; security clauses and audits to Unit 6; provider product details to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Virtual servers, virtual storage and usage monitors are the metered units that turn running resources into a bill. Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it compact.
chapters.depth: Virtual server as a guest with vCPU, RAM and disk on a hypervisor. Storage devices at billing level: block volume, object bucket, file share; note that Unit 4 covers their internal organisation. Usage monitor: metering samples, interval, aggregation, tags, quotas, chargeback, the link to billing. Mention that some syllabi call the usage monitor a metering service. Keep hypervisor internals out.

figure.title: Metered resources to invoice
figure.aria: A virtual CPU and RAM, a block volume and an object store feed a usage monitor, then an aggregator, then an invoice.

chapters.example: A VM has 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM and a 200 GB block volume. It runs for 10 hours. The meter samples every 5 minutes, so it takes 10 × 60 ÷ 5 = 120 samples. Prices are ₹6 per vCPU-hour, ₹1.5 per GB-hour of RAM, and ₹0.8 per GB-month for disk, with 730 hours in a month. CPU cost = 4 × 10 × ₹6 = ₹240. RAM cost = 16 × 10 × ₹1.5 = ₹240. Disk cost = 200 GB × (10 ÷ 730) month × ₹0.8 = ₹2.19. Total = ₹482.19.
chapters.trap: A stopped VM usually still bills its disk. Rounding and the sample interval change the total, and a host-level meter does not show which tenant used what without tags.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 for hypervisors and containers; chapter 2.1 for the data centre; Unit 4 for storage systems and billing models.
chapters.leave: Hypervisor implementation to Unit 3; GFS, HDFS and cloud databases to Unit 4; encryption and tenant isolation to Unit 6.
